title: Flu Season Arrived Early — and Texas Is Among the Hardest-Hit States
excerpt: This year's flu season did not wait for winter — and Texas is now one of seven states where the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention rates flu activity as high or very high.
content:
This year's flu season did not wait for winter — and Texas is now one of seven states where the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention rates flu activity as high or very high.

In its weekly FluView update on Friday, Nov. 13, the CDC reported that flu activity jumped from two states at high activity to seven in a single week: California, Louisiana, Oregon, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Washington. Outpatient visits for flu-like illness reached 3.2 percent, above the 2.9 percent national baseline that signals the season is underway in earnest.

The CDC now estimates at least 2.6 million flu illnesses, 36,000 hospitalizations and 2,100 deaths so far this season. Five children have died of flu this season, two of them added in the latest weekly report. Flu test positivity rose to 11.3 percent in the week ending Nov. 7, up from 9.1 percent the week before.

The surge is being driven by influenza A, mostly a mutated H1N1 strain — subclade D.3.1.1 — which made up 97.7 percent of subtyped influenza A samples from public health laboratories. Activity began rising in late August and early September, weeks ahead of the usual calendar. The CDC also noted that flu hospitalizations in mid-October were the highest seen that early in an autumn in more than 15 years.

The CDC was careful not to predict how bad the season will get. "An earlier increase in activity does not necessarily lead to a higher seasonal peak or greater overall severity," the agency said, and its preliminary severity assessment still rates the season as low across all age groups. The CDC expects the 2026-27 respiratory illness season to be much like last season.

The 2026-27 flu vaccine is available for everyone aged 6 months and older, according to the CDC.
